title: Die sieben Schwaben
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 119. Text from Wikisource („Die sieben Schwaben (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly. The narration is High German; the tale's eight rhymed couplets are broad Swabian dialect, glossed with their High German equivalents.
about: KHM 119 (Die sieben Schwaben) is a mock-heroic send-up of seven Swabians — Herr Schulz, Jackli, Marli, Jergli, Michal, Hans and Veitli — who arm themselves with a single spear, shared by all seven at once, and set off to find adventure and glory. Every escalation of danger is met with more bluster than courage: a buzzing beetle in the dusk is taken for an armed enemy and routs them in a panic, and a sleeping hare in a field is debated at cowardly length as a dragon before it simply hops away. Eight passages of dialogue break into broad Swabian dialect — the narration itself stays High German throughout — culminating in the party's end: unable to make themselves understood by a ferryman across the Moselle, they mishear his dialect “wat? wat?” as an order to wade across, and Herr Schulz, then, following his floating hat and a croaking frog, the other six after him, wade in and drown one by one. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as daß, gieng, Rath, erschrack and thun.

sentences.t: Einmal waren sieben Schwaben beisammen, der erste war der Herr Schulz, der zweite der Jackli, der dritte der Marli, der vierte der Jergli, der fünfte der Michal, der sechste der Hans, der siebente der Veitli;
sentences.l: Once seven Swabians were together, the first was Herr Schulz, the second [was] the Jackli, the third [was] the Marli, the fourth [was] the Jergli, the fifth [was] the Michal, the sixth [was] the Hans, the seventh [was] the Veitli;
sentences.i: Once seven Swabians were together: the first was Herr Schulz, the second Jackli, the third Marli, the fourth Jergli, the fifth Michal, the sixth Hans, the seventh Veitli;
sentences.n: German drops the verb after the first member of a list, so the bracketed “was” in the literal is supplied here and is not in the 1857 text. The names all carry the southern pet ending -li (Jackli from Jakob, Jergli from Georg, Veitli from Veit), and each takes the definite article, der Jackli, as southern speech does with names. Schulz is not a surname but the village headman’s title, short for Schultheiß, which is why he alone is a Herr.

sentences.t: die hatten alle siebene sich vorgenommen die Welt zu durchziehen, Abenteuer zu suchen und große Thaten zu vollbringen.
sentences.l: these had all seven of them purposed to travel through the world, to seek adventures and to accomplish great deeds.
sentences.i: All seven of them had resolved to travel through the world, to seek adventures and to do great deeds.
sentences.n: die at the head is a demonstrative, “these,” a favourite way of carrying a sentence on. siebene is the older emphatic form of sieben. sich vornehmen is “to resolve, to purpose,” with the reflexive in the dative. Thaten is the 1857 spelling of Taten.

sentences.t: Damit sie aber auch mit bewaffneter Hand und sicher giengen, sahen sies für gut an, daß sie sich zwar nur einen einzigen aber recht starken und langen Spieß machen ließen.
sentences.l: But so that they should go with armed hand and in safety, they saw it for good that they had made for themselves only one single but right strong and long spear.
sentences.i: But so that they might go armed and in safety, they thought it good to have a single spear made for them — only the one, but a right strong and long one.
sentences.n: damit is the conjunction “so that.” etwas für gut ansehen is “to judge a thing good”; ansehen is separable, so an closes the clause, and sies is sie es. sich machen lassen is the causative with a dative of interest, “to have made for oneself.” zwar … aber sets up the concession: only one, but a mighty one.

sentences.t: Diesen Spieß faßten sie alle siebene zusammen an, vorn gieng der kühnste und männlichste, das mußte der Herr Schulz sein, und dann folgten die andern nach der Reihe und der Veitli war der letzte.
sentences.l: This spear they all seven took hold of together, in front went the boldest and most manly, that had to be Herr Schulz, and then the others followed in their order and the Veitli was the last.
sentences.i: All seven took hold of this spear together; in front went the boldest and manliest, which had to be Herr Schulz, and then the others followed in their order, and Veitli was the last.
sentences.n: The object leads — Diesen Spieß — which puts the verb in second place and the subject after it; German can begin with whatever matters most. anfassen is separable: faßten … an. das mußte der Herr Schulz sein has the dry force of “it could hardly be anyone else.”

sentences.t: Nun geschah es, als sie im Heumonat eines Tags einen weiten Weg gegangen waren, auch noch ein gut Stück bis in das Dorf hatten, wo sie über Nacht bleiben mußten, daß in der Dämmerung auf einer Wiese ein großer Roßkäfer oder eine Hornisse nicht weit von ihnen hinter einer Staude vorbeiflog und feindlich brummelte.
sentences.l: Now it happened, when they had gone a long way one day in the hay-month, and had still a good stretch to the village where they had to stay overnight, that in the twilight on a meadow a great dung-beetle or a hornet flew past not far from them from behind a bush and droned in hostile fashion.
sentences.i: Now it came to pass, when they had gone a long way one day in the hay-month, and had still a good stretch to the village where they were to spend the night, that in the dusk, on a meadow, a great dung-beetle or a hornet flew past not far from them from behind a bush, buzzing at them angrily.
sentences.n: The frame is Nun geschah es … daß …, “now it happened that,” with two long time-clauses pushed in between, so the daß-clause that carries the news does not arrive until the end; hold the sentence open until it comes. Heumonat is July, the hay-month, and eines Tags is a genitive of time, “one day.” Roßkäfer — “horse-beetle” — is the big dung-beetle, and brummeln is a low continuous droning.

sentences.t: Der Herr Schulz erschrack, daß er fast den Spieß hätte fallen lassen und ihm der Angstschweiß am ganzen Leibe ausbrach.
sentences.l: Herr Schulz was frightened, so that he would almost have let the spear fall and the sweat of fear broke out on him over his whole body.
sentences.i: Herr Schulz was so frightened that he almost let the spear fall, and the sweat of fear broke out all over his body.
sentences.n: erschrack is the old past of erschrecken (modern erschrak). The daß-clause gives the degree of the fright. ihm is the dative of the person concerned where English uses a possessive — “his whole body.” Angstschweiß is fear-sweat, a compound of just its parts.

sentences.t: „Horcht, horcht,“ rief er seinen Gesellen, „Gott, ich höre eine Trommel!“
sentences.l: “Hark, hark,” he cried to his companions, “God, I hear a drum!”
sentences.i: “Listen, listen,” he cried to his fellows, “God, I hear a drum!”
sentences.n: horcht is the plural imperative of horchen, “to hearken.” seinen Gesellen is a bare dative, “to his companions,” with no preposition to help. What he hears is the beetle.

sentences.t: Der Jackli, der hinter ihm den Spieß hielt und dem ich weiß nicht was für ein Geruch in die Nase kam, sprach „etwas ist ohne Zweifel vorhanden, denn ich schmeck das Pulver und den Zündstrick.“
sentences.l: The Jackli, who held the spear behind him and into whose nose I know not what kind of smell came, said “something is without doubt at hand, for I smell the powder and the slow-match.”
sentences.i: Jackli, who held the spear behind him and into whose nose there came I know not what sort of smell, said, “something is afoot beyond doubt, for I smell powder and slow-match.”
sentences.n: The teller slips his own aside into the relative clause: dem … ich weiß nicht was für ein Geruch in die Nase kam. schmecken is used for smelling here, as southern speech does. A Zündstrick is the slow-burning cord that fired an old gun, so powder and match together mean an army.

sentences.t: Bei diesen Worten hub der Herr Schulz an die Flucht zu ergreifen, und sprang im Hui über einen Zaun,
sentences.l: At these words Herr Schulz began to seize flight, and sprang in a whisk over a fence,
sentences.i: At these words Herr Schulz set about taking to his heels, and sprang over a fence in a trice,
sentences.n: hub … an is the old past of anheben, “to begin” (modern hob an), with the particle standing apart. die Flucht ergreifen — “to seize flight” — is the set phrase for taking to one’s heels. im Hui is “in a whisk, in a flash.”

sentences.t: weil er aber gerade auf die Zinken eines Rechen sprang, der vom Heumachen da liegen geblieben war, so fuhr ihm der Stiel ins Gesicht und gab ihm einen ungewaschenen Schlag.
sentences.l: but because he sprang just upon the prongs of a rake that had stayed lying there from the hay-making, the handle flew into his face and gave him an unwashed blow.
sentences.i: but as he sprang right onto the prongs of a rake that had been left lying there from the hay-making, the handle flew up into his face and dealt him a blow that was no gentle one.
sentences.n: liegen bleiben, “to stay lying,” is the German for a thing left where it fell. ein ungewaschener Schlag — literally “an unwashed blow” — is an old turn for a rough, unceremonious knock; the same word is used of coarse talk.

sentences.t: „O wei, o wei,“ schrie der Herr Schulz, „nimm mich gefangen, ich ergeb mich, ich ergeb mich!“
sentences.l: “O woe, o woe,” cried Herr Schulz, “take me prisoner, I give myself up, I give myself up!”
sentences.i: “Oh woe, oh woe,” cried Herr Schulz, “take me prisoner, I surrender, I surrender!”
sentences.n: o wei is the cry of pain, the same word as our “woe.” gefangen nehmen is “to take captive”; sich ergeben is “to surrender,” and ergeb has dropped its final -e. He is surrendering to a rake.

sentences.t: Die andern sechs hüpften auch alle einer über den andern herzu und schrien „gibst du dich, so geb ich mich auch, gibst du dich, so geb ich mich auch.“
sentences.l: The other six also all hopped up hither one over the other and cried “if you give yourself up, then I give myself up too, if you give yourself up, then I give myself up too.”
sentences.i: The other six all came hopping up, one over the other, and cried, “if you surrender, then I surrender too; if you surrender, then I surrender too.”
sentences.n: einer über den andern is “one over the other,” a tangle of bodies, and herzu, “hither up,” closes the clause. sich geben is the short form of sich ergeben, and gibst du dich is again a conditional with the verb first and no wenn.

sentences.t: Endlich, wie kein Feind da war, der sie binden und fortführen wollte, merkten sie daß sie betrogen waren:
sentences.l: At last, when no enemy was there who wanted to bind them and lead them away, they noticed that they were deceived:
sentences.i: At last, when there was no enemy there to bind them and lead them away, they saw that they had been fooled:
sentences.n: wie is again “when.” wollte of a purpose is “was there to, meant to.” betrogen sein uses sein where English wants the perfect passive, “had been taken in.”

sentences.t: und damit die Geschichte nicht unter die Leute käme, und sie nicht genarrt und gespottet würden, verschwuren sie sich unter einander so lang davon still zu schweigen, bis einer unverhofft das Maul aufthäte.
sentences.l: and so that the story should not come among the people, and they should not be made fools of and mocked, they swore together among one another to keep silent about it so long, until one of them unexpectedly should open his mouth.
sentences.i: and so that the story should not get about among people, and they should not be made fools of and mocked, they swore to one another to keep silent about it until one of them should unexpectedly open his mouth.
sentences.n: käme, würden and aufthäte are subjunctives of the thing feared and the thing merely supposed. sich verschwören is “to swear together, to conspire.” aufthäte is the 1857 spelling of auftäte, from aufthun, “to open.” The last clause is the fuse of the joke: the oath holds only until somebody talks.

sentences.t: Hierauf zogen sie weiter.
sentences.l: Thereupon they moved on further.
sentences.i: Thereupon they journeyed on.
sentences.n: hierauf is “upon this, thereupon.” weiterziehen is separable, weiter closing the clause; ziehen of travellers is to journey.

sentences.t: Die zweite Gefährlichkeit, die sie erlebten, kann aber mit der ersten nicht verglichen werden.
sentences.l: The second perilousness that they experienced cannot, however, be compared with the first.
sentences.i: The second peril they went through, however, is not to be compared with the first.
sentences.n: Gefährlichkeit is not the usual Gefahr but the abstract noun made from gefährlich — the tale’s mock-solemn way of numbering their adventures. The present tense (kann) steps out of the story to speak to the hearer.

sentences.t: Nach etlichen Tagen trug sie ihr Weg durch ein Brachfeld, da saß ein Hase in der Sonne und schlief, streckte die Ohren in die Höhe, und hatte die großen gläsernen Augen starr aufstehen.
sentences.l: After several days their way carried them through a fallow field, there sat a hare in the sun and slept, stretched its ears into the height, and had its great glassy eyes standing rigidly open.
sentences.i: After several days their way carried them through a fallow field, and there sat a hare in the sun asleep, its ears stretched up on end, and its great glassy eyes standing rigidly open.
sentences.n: trug sie ihr Weg — the way is the subject and carries them, a turn German likes. Brachfeld is land lying fallow. hatte … aufstehen is the old construction of haben with a bare infinitive, “had them standing open.”

sentences.t: Da erschraken sie bei dem Anblick des grausamen und wilden Thieres insgesammt und hielten Rath was zu thun das wenigst gefährliche wäre.
sentences.l: Then they all together took fright at the sight of the cruel and wild beast and held counsel what would be the least dangerous to do.
sentences.i: Then they were all together frightened at the sight of the fierce and savage beast, and held counsel as to what would be the least dangerous thing to do.
sentences.n: Rath halten is “to hold counsel”; Rath and Thier are the 1857 spellings of Rat and Tier. insgesammt is “all together, to a man.” The beast is a sleeping hare: grausam and wild are the Swabians’ estimate, not the tale’s.

sentences.t: Denn so sie fliehen wollten, war zu besorgen, das Ungeheuer setzte ihnen nach und verschlänge sie alle mit Haut und Haar.
sentences.l: For if they wanted to flee, it was to be feared the monster would set after them and would devour them all with skin and hair.
sentences.i: For if they chose to flee, it was to be feared the monster would come after them and swallow them all, hide and hair.
sentences.n: so at the head of a clause is an old “if.” war zu besorgen is “was to be feared,” the sein + zu turn that English renders with a passive. nachsetzen is separable, “to set after.” verschlänge is the subjunctive of verschlingen, and mit Haut und Haar is the fixed phrase for utterly.

sentences.t: Also sprachen sie „wir müssen einen großen und gefährlichen Kampf bestehen, frisch gewagt ist halb gewonnen!“
sentences.l: So they spoke “we must stand through a great and dangerous fight, boldly ventured is half won!”
sentences.i: So they said, “we must go through a great and perilous fight — a thing boldly begun is half won!”
sentences.n: einen Kampf bestehen is to stand a fight through, to see it out. The proverb frisch gewagt ist halb gewonnen is the same one the little tailor speaks in KHM 114; here it is said over a sleeping hare.

sentences.t: faßten alle siebene den Spieß an, der Herr Schulz vorn und der Veitli hinten.
sentences.l: took hold all seven of the spear, Herr Schulz in front and the Veitli behind.
sentences.i: and all seven took hold of the spear, Herr Schulz in front and Veitli behind.
sentences.n: The subject is left out and the verb comes first, running straight on from the speech before — the pace of spoken telling. The second half has no verb at all, and English must either supply one or let it stand as a phrase.

sentences.t: Der Herr Schulz wollte den Spieß noch immer anhalten, der Veitli aber war hinten ganz muthig geworden, wollte losbrechen und rief
sentences.l: Herr Schulz wanted still always to hold the spear back, but the Veitli had at the rear grown quite courageous, wanted to break loose and cried
sentences.i: Herr Schulz still wanted to hold the spear back, but Veitli, at the rear, had grown quite bold, wanted to break loose, and cried
sentences.n: anhalten here is “to hold back, to check,” not the modern “to stop.” muthig is the 1857 spelling of mutig. Courage in this tale is measured by distance from the hare.

sentences.t:
„stoß zu in aller Schwabe Name,
sonst wünsch i, daß ihr möcht erlahme.“
sentences.l:
“thrust home in all Swabians’ name,
else I wish that you may go lame.”
sentences.i:
“Thrust home, in the name of all Swabians,
or else I wish that you may be struck lame.”
sentences.n: All eight couplets in this tale are in broad Swabian, and each rhymes (here Name/erlahme); Lectorium’s idiomatic line does not try to keep the rhyme. stoß zu is the imperative of zustoßen, “thrust home,” and not the noun Stoß. i is Swabian for ich. Schwabe is the genitive plural, aller Schwaben. Swabian regularly drops the final -n of an infinitive: erlahme for erlahmen, “to go lame.”

sentences.t: Aber der Hans wußt ihn zu treffen und sprach
sentences.l: But the Hans knew how to hit him and said
sentences.i: But Hans knew how to hit him, and said
sentences.n: wußt is the short past of wissen, and wissen zu with an infinitive is “to know how to.” treffen is to hit him with a word — the same verb that means hitting a mark.

sentences.t:
„beim Element, du hascht gut schwätze,
bischt stets der letscht beim Drachehetze.“
sentences.l:
“by the element, you have good talking,
you are ever the last at the dragon-baiting.”
sentences.i:
“By the elements, it is easy for you to talk —
you are always the last when a dragon is to be hunted.”
sentences.n: The Swabian -scht for -st runs through the dialect: hascht for hast, bischt for bist, letscht for letzte. du hascht gut schwätze is “you have good talking,” the German way of saying it is easy for you to talk; schwätze drops the -n of schwätzen. beim Element is a mild oath. Drachehetze is Drachenhetze, the baiting of a dragon.

sentences.t: Der Michal rief
sentences.l: The Michal cried
sentences.n: The southern definite article before a name once more: der Michal.

sentences.t:
„es wird nit fehle um ei Haar,
so ischt es wohl der Teufel gar.“
sentences.l:
“it will not fail by a hair,
so it is surely the devil no less.”
sentences.i:
“It will not be out by a hair’s breadth —
then it is the devil himself.”
sentences.n: nit is Swabian for nicht, fehle for fehlen with the -n dropped, and ei for ein: the dialect thins the diphthong. ischt is ist. gar here is the intensifier “downright, no less,” not the gar of gar nicht.

sentences.t: Drauf kam an den Jergli die Reihe der sprach
sentences.l: Thereupon the turn came to the Jergli, who said
sentences.i: Thereupon it came to Jergli’s turn, and he said
sentences.n: an jemanden kommt die Reihe is “it is someone’s turn.” The der at the end is a demonstrative doing a relative pronoun’s work — “that one, he” — and the 1857 text sets no comma before it.

sentences.t:
„ischt er es nit, so ischts sei Muter
oder des Teufels Stiefbruder.“
sentences.l:
“if he is not it, then it is his mother
or the devil’s stepbrother.”
sentences.i:
“If it is not he, then it is his mother,
or else the devil’s stepbrother.”
sentences.n: sei is Swabian for sein or seine, “his,” and not the imperative of sein. ischts is ist es. Muter is Mutter written with a single t as it is spoken for the rhyme. ischt er es nit is again a conditional with the verb first.

sentences.t: Der Marli hatte da einen guten Gedanken und sagte zum Veitli
sentences.l: The Marli had then a good thought and said to the Veitli
sentences.i: Marli then had a good thought, and said to Veitli
sentences.n: einen Gedanken haben is to hit on an idea; the idea, as it turns out, is to send Veitli first.

sentences.t:
„gang, Veitli, gang, gang du voran,
i will dahinte vor di stahn.“
sentences.l:
“go, Veitli, go, go you in front,
I will behind stand before you.”
sentences.i:
“Go, Veitli, go, go you in front —
I will stand in front of you, from behind.”
sentences.n: gang is the Swabian imperative of gehen, “go,” and not the noun Gang. i is ich, dahinte is dahinten, di is dich, and stahn is stehen. The second line is the tale’s joke in one breath: he offers to stand in front of Veitli while staying behind him.

sentences.t: Der Veitli hörte aber nicht drauf und der Jackli sagte
sentences.l: But the Veitli did not listen to it and the Jackli said
sentences.i: But Veitli would not hear of it, and Jackli said
sentences.n: auf etwas hören is “to listen to, to heed,” and drauf is darauf, “to that.”

sentences.t:
„der Schulz, der muß der erschte sei,
denn ihm gebührt die Ehr allei.“
sentences.l:
“the Schulz, he must be the first,
for to him the honour is due alone.”
sentences.i:
“Herr Schulz must be the first,
for the honour belongs to him alone.”
sentences.n: erschte is erste with the Swabian -scht; sei is the infinitive sein with its -n dropped; Ehr is Ehre and allei is allein. gebühren takes the dative: ihm gebührt, “is due to him.” Schulz is the office of village headman, not a family name, which is why the honour is his.

sentences.t: Da nahm sich der Herr Schulz ein Herz und sprach gravitätisch
sentences.l: Then Herr Schulz took himself a heart and spoke gravely
sentences.i: Then Herr Schulz took heart, and said with great gravity
sentences.n: sich ein Herz nehmen is “to take heart,” with the reflexive in the dative. gravitätisch comes from Latin gravitas, and the tale is smiling at his dignity.

sentences.t:
„so zieht denn herzhaft in den Streit,
hieran erkennt man tapfre Leut.“
sentences.l:
“so march then stoutly into the strife,
by this one knows brave folk.”
sentences.i:
“Then march stoutly into the fight —
this is how brave folk are known.”
sentences.n: This couplet is almost High German — only Leut for Leute and tapfre for tapfere carry the dialect — because Herr Schulz is speaking in his official voice. hieran is “by this,” and erkennt man is the impersonal “one recognises.”

sentences.t: Da giengen sie insgesammt auf den Drachen los.
sentences.l: Then they all together went at the dragon.
sentences.i: Then all together they made at the dragon.
sentences.n: losgehen auf is “to go at, to make for” an enemy. In their own telling the hare has now become a Drache, a dragon. giengen is the 1857 spelling of gingen.

sentences.t: Der Herr Schulz segnete sich und rief Gott um Beistand an:
sentences.l: Herr Schulz blessed himself and called on God for assistance:
sentences.i: Herr Schulz crossed himself and called upon God for aid:
sentences.n: sich segnen is to make the sign of the cross over oneself. anrufen, “to call upon,” is separable, so an closes the clause; um Beistand names what is asked for.

sentences.t: wie aber das alles nicht helfen wollte und er dem Feind immer näher kam, schrie er in großer Angst „hau! hurlehau! hau! hauhau!“
sentences.l: but when all that would not help and he came ever nearer to the enemy, he cried in great fear “hau! hurlehau! hau! hauhau!”
sentences.i: but when all that was of no use and he came nearer and nearer to the foe, he cried out in great fear, “hau! hurlehau! hau! hauhau!”
sentences.n: nicht helfen wollen is “to be of no use.” hau is the imperative of hauen, “strike,” but strung out like this the war-cry is panic rather than words, and it is left as it stands.

sentences.t: Davon erwachte der Has, erschrack und sprang eilig davon.
sentences.l: From that the hare awoke, took fright and sprang hastily away.
sentences.i: At that the hare awoke, took fright, and sprang hastily away.
sentences.n: davon at the head is “from that,” while the davon at the end belongs to davonspringen, “to spring away”: the same two syllables doing two different pieces of work in one sentence. Has is the short old form of Hase.

sentences.t: Als ihn der Herr Schulz so feldflüchtig sah, da rief er voll Freude
sentences.l: When Herr Schulz saw him so field-fleeing, he cried full of joy
sentences.i: When Herr Schulz saw him thus in flight from the field, he cried out full of joy
sentences.n: feldflüchtig — “field-fleeing” — is a soldier’s word for one who runs from the battlefield; the hare is granted the full military dignity of a rout.

sentences.t:
„potz, Veitli, lueg, lueg, was isch das?
das Ungehüer ischt a Has.“
sentences.l:
“potz, Veitli, look, look, what is that?
the monster is a hare.”
sentences.i:
“Good gracious, Veitli, look, look, what is that?
The monster is a hare.”
sentences.n: potz is a softened oath, as in potz Blitz. lueg is Swabian for schau; isch and ischt are both ist; a is ein; Ungehüer is Ungeheuer, and Has the short Hase. The whole tale has been walking toward this line.

sentences.t: Der Schwabenbund suchte aber weiter Abenteuer und kam an die Mosel, ein mosiges, stilles und tiefes Wasser, darüber nicht viel Brücken sind, sondern man an mehrern Orten sich muß in Schiffen überfahren lassen.
sentences.l: But the Swabian league sought adventures further and came to the Mosel, a mossy, still and deep water, over which there are not many bridges, but one must in several places have oneself ferried across in boats.
sentences.i: But the Swabian league sought further adventures and came to the Moselle, a mossy, still and deep water, over which there are not many bridges, so that in several places one must have oneself ferried across in boats.
sentences.n: Schwabenbund plays on the historical Swabian League, a real alliance of towns and knights. mosig is “mossy,” and the tale is playing on the name Mosel. sich überfahren lassen is the causative again, “to have oneself carried across.” mehrern is the older form of mehreren.

sentences.t: Weil die sieben Schwaben dessen unberichtet waren, riefen sie einem Mann, der jenseits des Wassers seine Arbeit vollbrachte, zu, wie man doch hinüber kommen könnte?
sentences.l: Because the seven Swabians were uninformed of this, they called across to a man who was doing his work on the far side of the water, how one might get over?
sentences.i: Since the seven Swabians knew nothing of this, they called across to a man who was at his work on the far side of the water, asking how one might get over.
sentences.n: dessen unberichtet sein is “to be uninformed of it,” with the genitive dessen. zurufen is separable, and its zu waits through the whole relative clause before it lands. The 1857 text keeps the question mark although the question is reported.

sentences.t: Der Mann verstand wegen der Weite und wegen ihrer Sprache nicht was sie wollten, und fragte auf sein trierisch „wat? wat?“
sentences.l: The man did not understand, on account of the distance and on account of their speech, what they wanted, and asked in his Trier way “wat? wat?”
sentences.i: The man, what with the distance and what with their speech, did not understand what they wanted, and asked in his Trier dialect, “wat? wat?”
sentences.n: die Weite here is the noun, the distance, not the adjective “wide.” auf sein trierisch is “in his Trier fashion” — the speech of Trier on the Moselle, which says wat where High German says was. The tale sets one dialect against another: Swabian on the one bank, Moselle Franconian on the other.

sentences.t: Da meinte der Herr Schulz er spräche nicht anders als „wade, wade durchs Wasser,“ und hub an, weil er der Vorderste war, sich auf den Weg zu machen und in die Mosel hineinzugehen.
sentences.l: Then Herr Schulz thought he was saying nothing other than “wade, wade through the water,” and began, because he was the foremost, to set out on the way and to go into the Mosel.
sentences.i: Then Herr Schulz supposed he was saying nothing else than, “wade, wade through the water,” and, being the foremost, he set about starting off and walking into the Moselle.
sentences.n: spräche is the subjunctive of reported thought. Herr Schulz hears the Trier man’s wat, wat as wade, wade, the imperative of waten, “to wade” — the mishearing that drowns them all. hub an is once more the old past of anheben.

sentences.t: Nicht lang, so versank er in den Schlamm und in die antreibenden tiefen Wellen, seinen Hut aber jagte der Wind hinüber an das jenseitige Ufer, und ein Frosch setzte sich dabei und quackte „wat, wat, wat.“
sentences.l: Not long, and he sank into the mud and into the driving deep waves, but his hat the wind chased over to the far bank, and a frog set itself beside it and croaked “wat, wat, wat.”
sentences.i: It was not long before he sank into the mud and the deep driving waves; but his hat the wind drove across to the far bank, and a frog settled beside it and croaked, “wat, wat, wat.”
sentences.n: Nicht lang, so … is the short old formula, “it was not long before.” seinen Hut stands first as the object, which puts the verb ahead of its subject: “his hat the wind chased.” antreibend is “driving on, drifting.” The frog now says exactly what the man of Trier said.

sentences.t: Die sechs andern hörten das drüben und sprachen „unser Gesell, der Herr Schulz, ruft uns, kann er hinüber waden, warum wir nicht auch?“
sentences.l: The six others heard that from over there and said “our fellow, Herr Schulz, is calling us, if he can wade across, why not we too?”
sentences.i: The six others heard it from the other side and said, “our fellow Herr Schulz is calling us; if he can wade across, why should not we?”
sentences.n: waden is the tale’s spelling of waten, “to wade,” and has nothing to do with die Waden, the calves of the leg. The verb is left out in warum wir nicht auch, just as it is in the English “why not we.”

sentences.t: Sprangen darum eilig alle zusammen in das Wasser und ertranken, also daß ein Frosch ihrer sechse ums Leben brachte, und niemand von dem Schwabenbund wieder nach Haus kam.
sentences.l: Sprang therefore hastily all together into the water and drowned, so that a frog brought six of them out of life, and nobody of the Swabian league came home again.
sentences.i: So they all sprang hastily together into the water and drowned, so that one frog brought six of them to their death, and not one of the Swabian league ever came home again.
sentences.n: The subject is left out again at the start, as it was earlier in faßten. ihrer sechse is the old partitive genitive, “six of them.” ums Leben bringen is “to bring out of life,” to kill. The tale ends without a word of pity — and counts six, because the seventh had already drowned.

glossary.a: ein — a, an (Swabian a = ein; das Ungehüer ischt a Has)
glossary.anhalten: anhalten — to hold back, to check (infinitive; separable — the older sense, not the modern “to stop”)
glossary.aufstehen: aufstehen — to stand open (of eyes, after haben with a bare infinitive: hatte die Augen aufstehen; elsewhere to get up, rise)
glossary.besorgen: besorgen — to fear, to apprehend (infinitive; zu besorgen sein: to be feared — the older sense, not “to see to”)
glossary.ehr: die Ehre — the honour (Swabian Ehr = Ehre)
glossary.ei: ein — a, one (Swabian ei = ein; um ei Haar: by a hair’s breadth)
glossary.gar: gar — downright, no less (intensifier; der Teufel gar: the devil himself)
glossary.gedanken: der Gedanke — thought (acc. sg. of the weak noun; einen Gedanken haben: to hit on an idea)
glossary.ihrer: ihrer — their (poss., gen.: wegen ihrer Sprache); also of them (partitive gen. of sie: ihrer sechse, six of them)
glossary.leut: die Leute — people, folk (Swabian Leut = Leute)
glossary.ließen: lassen — had (a thing) made (3rd pl. past; sich etwas machen lassen: to have something made for oneself)
glossary.los: losgehen — at, against (separable particle: auf jemanden losgehen, to go at someone — not los, “rid of”)
glossary.möcht: mögen — may (2nd pl. pres. subj. in a wish: daß ihr möcht erlahme; Swabian for möget)
glossary.reihe: die Reihe — row, order; a turn (nach der Reihe: in turn; an jemanden kommt die Reihe: it is someone’s turn)
glossary.sei: sein — his (Swabian sei = sein/seine); also sein — to be (the infinitive with its final -n dropped: der erschte sei)
glossary.setzte: setzen — set (3rd sg. past; sich setzen: to sit down; nachsetzen: to set after, pursue)
glossary.sies: sies — = sie es (they … it: sahen sies für gut an)
glossary.stoß: zustoßen — thrust home! (imperative; the particle follows: stoß zu)
glossary.thaten: die That — deeds (pl.; 1857 spelling of Taten — the noun, not the past of thun)
glossary.ungeheuer: das Ungeheuer — monster (noun; not the adverb ungeheuer, “hugely”)
glossary.verglichen: vergleichen — compared (past part.; mit etwas verglichen werden: to be compared with)
glossary.waden: waten — to wade (the tale’s spelling; not die Waden, the calves of the leg)
glossary.wat: was — what (the Trier dialect on the Moselle says wat for was)
glossary.weg: der Weg — way, road (the noun; not the adverb weg, “away”)
glossary.weite: die Weite — distance (noun; wegen der Weite: on account of the distance)
glossary.weiß: wissen — to know (1st/3rd sg. present; not the adjective weiß, white)
glossary.zieht: ziehen — march! set forth! (imperative pl.; ziehen of soldiers or travellers is to march, not to pull)
glossary.zinken: der Zinken — prongs, tines (pl.; here of a hay-rake)
glossary.zogen: ziehen — went, journeyed on (3rd pl. past; separable weiterziehen/fortziehen — not “pulled” here)
